about.title: Thousand Oaks Product Liability Claims
about.longDescription: A product is supposed to do its job without hurting you. When something you bought in Thousand Oaks — a space heater, a child's car seat, a power tool, a prescription bottle — fails in a way it never should have, California law puts the burden where it belongs. Under strict liability, you generally do not have to prove the manufacturer was careless. You show the product had a defect in its design, its manufacturing, or its warnings, and that the defect caused your injury. Vehicle components are part of this picture too. Public records logged 616 injury collisions in Thousand Oaks during 2025, with 859 people hurt, and a portion of those wrecks on US-101 or Moorpark Road may have involved an airbag, a tire, or a brake system that did not perform as promised. We handle product liability claims on contingency, so nothing is owed unless there is a recovery. Whatever went wrong, keep the product.

items.desc: The product itself is the heart of the case. We can help you secure it, along with packaging, receipts, and photos, before anything is lost or discarded.

items.question: My airbag did not deploy in a crash on the 101 near Hillcrest Drive. Is that a car accident claim or a product claim?
items.answer: It may be both. A collision case looks at how the other driver behaved, while a product liability claim asks whether the airbag, seatbelt, or another component had a defect that made your injuries worse. We can review the vehicle and the crash report to see whether the manufacturer should be part of your claim. Do not let the car be salvaged or repaired until it has been inspected.

items.question: I threw away the broken product. Can I still bring a claim?
items.answer: Losing the product makes a case harder, but it does not always end it. Photos, receipts, medical records, recall notices, and the same model purchased elsewhere can sometimes fill the gap. Talk with us before assuming the claim is gone.

items.question: Do I have to prove the company knew the product was faulty?
items.answer: Generally, no. California applies strict liability to many product cases, meaning the question is whether the product was defective in its design, manufacturing, or warnings and whether that defect caused your injury. What the company knew or intended is usually not something you have to establish. We can explain how this applies to your specific situation.
